claims.source: Additionally, the neurofibromin C-terminus is a positive regulator of G-protein-stimulated adenylyl cyclase activity (Hannan et al., 2006; Tong et al., 2002), and cAMP deficiency in NF1 knockout models causes altered in vitro neuronal morphology and growth, visual learning deficits, and changes in cortical architecture in mice (Brown et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2010b; Hegedus et al., 2007; Wolman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This causal relationship is stated in the introduction with citations to Brown et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2010b; Hegedus et al., 2007; Wolman et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Mesolimbic reward circuits involve the convergence of dopaminergic projections from the midbrain ventral tegmental area (VTA) with glutamatergic inputs from cortical and subcortical regions on medium spiny neurons in the nucleus accumbens (NAc).
claims.source: Mesolimbic reward circuits involve the convergence of dopaminergic projections from the midbrain ventral tegmental area (VTA) with glutamatergic inputs from cortical and subcortical regions on medium spiny neurons in the nucleus accumbens (NAc).
claims.evidence: This anatomical description is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about mesolimbic circuits.

claims.claim: Mesolimbic circuits facilitate the translation of relevant internal and external stimuli into motivated behaviors.
claims.source: These circuits facilitate the translation of relevant internal and external stimuli into motivated behaviors (Wise, 2005) and have been implicated in the pathophysiology of ADHD and other disorders of impulse control (Li et al., 2006; Purper-Ouakil et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This functional role is stated in the introduction with a citation to Wise, 2005.

claims.claim: Mesolimbic circuits have been implicated in the pathophysiology of ADHD and other disorders of impulse control.
claims.source: These circuits facilitate the translation of relevant internal and external stimuli into motivated behaviors (Wise, 2005) and have been implicated in the pathophysiology of ADHD and other disorders of impulse control (Li et al., 2006; Purper-Ouakil et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This implication is stated in the introduction with citations to Li et al., 2006 and Purper-Ouakil et al., 2011.

claims.claim: In the optic glioma mouse model of NF1, reduced striatal dopamine is associated with motor, exploratory, spatial learning, and attentional abnormalities.
claims.source: In the optic glioma mouse model of NF1 (OPG, a conditional Nf1 knockout in astrocytes on an Nf1+/- background), reduced striatal dopamine is associated with motor, exploratory, spatial learning, and attentional abnormalities (Brown et al., 2010a; Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013; Anastasaki et al., 2015), which are ameliorated by treatment with the catecholamine re-uptake inhibitor methylphenidate or the dopamine precursor L-DOPA (Brown et al., 2010a).
claims.evidence: This association is stated in the introduction with citations to Brown et al., 2010a; Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013; Anastasaki et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Motor, exploratory, spatial learning, and attentional abnormalities in the optic glioma mouse model are ameliorated by treatment with methylphenidate or L-DOPA.
claims.source: In the optic glioma mouse model of NF1 (OPG, a conditional Nf1 knockout in astrocytes on an Nf1+/- background), reduced striatal dopamine is associated with motor, exploratory, spatial learning, and attentional abnormalities (Brown et al., 2010a; Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013; Anastasaki et al., 2015), which are ameliorated by treatment with the catecholamine re-uptake inhibitor methylphenidate or the dopamine precursor L-DOPA (Brown et al., 2010a).
claims.evidence: This amelioration is stated in the introduction with a citation to Brown et al., 2010a.

claims.claim: Dopaminergic neurotransmission has never been investigated in NF1 models in vivo.
claims.source: Despite these efforts, dopaminergic neurotransmission has never been investigated in NF1 models in vivo.
claims.evidence: This gap in knowledge is explicitly stated in the introduction.

claims.claim: dLight1.2 allows for sub-micromolar detection of extracellular dopamine concentrations with sub-second resolution.
claims.source: In order to investigate dopamine dynamics in freely behaving Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice, we utilized the genetically encoded, fluorescent dopamine sensor dLight1.2 (Patriarchi et al., 2018), which allows for sub-micromolar detection of extracellular dopamine concentrations with sub-second resolution and negligible sensitivity to other monoamines, GABA, and glutamate (Corre et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This technical capability is stated in the Results section with citations to Corre et al., 2018 and Patriarchi et al., 2018.

claims.claim: dLight1.2 has negligible sensitivity to other monoamines, GABA, and glutamate.
claims.source: In order to investigate dopamine dynamics in freely behaving Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice, we utilized the genetically encoded, fluorescent dopamine sensor dLight1.2 (Patriarchi et al., 2018), which allows for sub-micromolar detection of extracellular dopamine concentrations with sub-second resolution and negligible sensitivity to other monoamines, GABA, and glutamate (Corre et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This specificity is stated in the Results section with citations to Corre et al., 2018 and Patriarchi et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The dopamine transient event rate was reduced in Nf1+/- mice compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
claims.source: Peak analysis was performed to identify local trace prominences (Figure 1D) and revealed that the dopamine transient event rate was reduced in Nf1+/- mice compared to Nf1+/+ littermates (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Baseline (median) fluorescence, peak amplitude, and full width at half maximal intensity (FWHM) were equivalent between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- genotypes.
claims.source: Baseline (median) fluorescence, peak amplitude, and full width at half maximal intensity (FWHM) was equivalent between genotypes.
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section based on peak analysis of dLight1.2 signals.

claims.claim: No differences in dopamine (DA), serotonin (5-HT), norepinephrine (NE), or their metabolites were detected between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- genotypes in the NAc.
claims.source: We failed to detect differences in dopamine (DA), serotonin (5-HT), norepinephrine (NE), or their metabolites between genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: There was no difference in dopaminergic terminal tyrosine hydroxylase expression across striatal sub-compartments between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice.
claims.source: Additionally, there was no difference in dopaminergic terminal tyrosine hydroxylase expression across striatal sub-compartments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Basal differences in dLight1.2 event rate are not due to changes in dopaminergic terminal density or dopamine synthetic capacity.
claims.source: These findings suggest that basal differences in dLight1.2 event rate are not due to changes in dopaminergic terminal density or dopamine synthetic capacity.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on HPLC and immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: Putative dopaminergic neurons in Nf1+/- midbrain slices exhibited lower spontaneous whole-cell firing rates compared to Nf1+/+ neurons.
claims.source: We found that putative dopaminergic neurons in Nf1+/- midbrain slices exhibited lower spontaneous whole-cell firing rates (Figure 1G) and required more rheobase current to elicit a spike when compared to Nf1+/+ neurons (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons required more rheobase current to elicit a spike compared to Nf1+/+ neurons.
claims.source: We found that putative dopaminergic neurons in Nf1+/- midbrain slices exhibited lower spontaneous whole-cell firing rates (Figure 1G) and required more rheobase current to elicit a spike when compared to Nf1+/+ neurons (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: Phenotypic differences in baseline dLight1.2 event metrics are activity-dependent.
claims.source: This finding supports the hypothesis that phenotypic differences in baseline dLight1.2 event metrics are activity-dependent.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on electrophysiology findings.

claims.claim: Action potential threshold, duration, amplitude, and after hyperpolarization magnitude did not differ between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- genotypes.
claims.source: Action potential threshold, duration, amplitude, and after hyperpolarization magnitude did not differ between genotypes (Figure 1I–J, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1I-J and Table 1.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons had increased input resistance (Rm) compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
claims.source: During whole-cell recordings, we also observed that Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons exhibit increased input resistance (Rm) and decreased membrane capacitance (Cm) compared to Nf1+/+ littermates (Figure 2A) without a change in other membrane properties (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons had decreased membrane capacitance (Cm) compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
claims.source: During whole-cell recordings, we also observed that Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons exhibit increased input resistance (Rm) and decreased membrane capacitance (Cm) compared to Nf1+/+ littermates (Figure 2A) without a change in other membrane properties (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Cross-sectional area, major axis length, and minor axis length of VTA dopaminergic somata were reduced in Nf1+/- mice.
claims.source: We found that cross-sectional area, major axis length, and minor axis length were reduced in Nf1+/- mice (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Soma aspect ratio was equivalent between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- genotypes.
claims.source: Proportionality was maintained, however, as the soma aspect ratio was equivalent between genotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: TH immunofluorescence and total neuron counts in the VTA did not differ between Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ dopaminergic neurons.
claims.source: TH immunofluorescence and total neuron counts in the VTA did not differ between Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ dopaminergic neurons (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: No phenotypic differences in soma size were observed in the adjacent substantia nigra pars compacta.
claims.source: No phenotypic differences were observed in the adjacent substantia nigra pars compacta (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Relative differences in soma size were VTA-specific.
claims.source: These findings indicate that relative differences in soma size were VTA-specific and could have contributed to changes in passive membrane properties.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on morphological analysis.

claims.claim: No difference in dendritic complexity or total neurite length was observed between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- genotypes.
claims.source: No difference in dendritic complexity or total neurite length was observed between genotypes (Figure 2H), which suggests that, although Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons have smaller somata than Nf1+/+ neurons, they have similar neurite morphology.
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons had smaller Ih current amplitudes compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
claims.source: We found that Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons had smaller Ih current amplitudes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) without a change in voltage dependence (Figure 3B; determined by tail current analysis) relative to Nf1+/+ littermates.
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: There was no change in Ih voltage dependence between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons.
claims.source: We found that Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons had smaller Ih current amplitudes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) without a change in voltage dependence (Figure 3B; determined by tail current analysis) relative to Nf1+/+ littermates.
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Differences in Ih current amplitudes were not significant when normalized to cell capacitance.
claims.source: Differences in Ih current amplitudes were not significant when normalized to the cell capacitance to account for cell size (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and maximum Ih current amplitude was significantly correlated with Cm across all animals and within genotypes (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Maximum Ih current amplitude was significantly correlated with Cm across all animals and within genotypes.
claims.source: Differences in Ih current amplitudes were not significant when normalized to the cell capacitance to account for cell size (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and maximum Ih current amplitude was significantly correlated with Cm across all animals and within genotypes (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Addition of 20 µM forskolin to the bath solution did not significantly affect Ih magnitude or voltage dependence in Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons.
claims.source: Addition of 20 µM forskolin to the bath solution did not significantly affect Ih magnitude or voltage dependence in Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Changes in Ih magnitude are likely cAMP-independent and reflective of smaller cell size.
claims.source: Thus, changes in Ih magnitude are likely cAMP-independent, reflective of smaller cell size, and unlikely to be the etiologic cause of reduced cell excitability.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on forskolin experiments.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons displayed increased sIPSC frequency compared to Nf1+/+ neurons.
claims.source: We found that Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons displayed increased sIPSC frequency but not sIPSC amplitude, sEPSC frequency, or sEPSC amplitude compared to Nf1+/+ neurons (Figure 3F–G).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claims.claim: No differences in sIPSC amplitude, sEPSC frequency, or sEPSC amplitude were observed between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- neurons.
claims.source: We found that Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons displayed increased sIPSC frequency but not sIPSC amplitude, sEPSC frequency, or sEPSC amplitude compared to Nf1+/+ neurons (Figure 3F–G).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claims.claim: Addition of 100 µM picrotoxin to the bath solution rescued spontaneous firing rates in Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons.
claims.source: Addition of 100 µM picrotoxin (a highly selective, non-competitive GABAA receptor antagonist) to the bath solution rescued spontaneous firing rates in Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons (Figure 3H) without affecting passive membrane properties (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: Picrotoxin reduced rheobase to levels significantly lower than control- and picrotoxin-treated Nf1+/+ cells.
claims.source: Picrotoxin also reduced rheobase to levels significantly lower than control- and picrotoxin-treated Nf1+/+ cells (Figure 3I), which would be expected at baseline due to differences in soma volume.
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: Pre-treating Nf1+/- mice with morphine sulfate (5 mg/kg, s.c.) raised spontaneous dLight1.2 transient event rate.
claims.source: We found that pre-treating Nf1+/- mice with the mu opioid receptor agonist morphine sulfate (5 mg/kg, s.c.) raised spontaneous dLight1.2 transient event rate but not event magnitude or FWHM relative to saline (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Morphine sulfate did not affect dLight1.2 event magnitude or FWHM in Nf1+/- mice.
claims.source: We found that pre-treating Nf1+/- mice with the mu opioid receptor agonist morphine sulfate (5 mg/kg, s.c.) raised spontaneous dLight1.2 transient event rate but not event magnitude or FWHM relative to saline (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Excitation/inhibition imbalance is a mechanism gating Nf1+/- dopaminergic excitability ex vivo.
claims.source: Thus, excitation/inhibition imbalance is a mechanism gating Nf1+/- dopaminergic excitability ex vivo, and attenuation of VTA GABAergic neurotransmission normalizes spontaneous LNAc dopaminergic neurotransmission in vivo.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on picrotoxin and morphine experiments.

claims.claim: Attenuation of VTA GABAergic neurotransmission normalizes spontaneous LNAc dopaminergic neurotransmission in vivo.
claims.source: Thus, excitation/inhibition imbalance is a mechanism gating Nf1+/- dopaminergic excitability ex vivo, and attenuation of VTA GABAergic neurotransmission normalizes spontaneous LNAc dopaminergic neurotransmission in vivo.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on morphine experiments.

claims.claim: Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice observed robust LNAc dopamine transients time-locked to reward consumption that were not significantly different between genotypes.
claims.source: In both Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ mice, we observed robust LNAc dopamine transients time-locked to reward consumption (Figure 4A) that were not significantly different between genotypes (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claims.claim: No difference in the number of rewards consumed during the 30 min session was observed between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- groups.
claims.source: No difference in the number of rewards consumed during the 30 min session was observed between groups (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Large dopamine transients were observed at the onset of interaction with a novel, sex-matched, juvenile conspecific that was independent of genotype.
claims.source: We observed large transients at the onset of interaction with a novel, sex-matched, juvenile conspecific that was independent of genotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ littermates failed to display differences in preference for a novel mouse in a social preference task.
claims.source: Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ littermates also failed to display differences in preference for a novel mouse in a social preference task (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: LNAc dopamine and behavioral responses to unconditioned rewards are preserved in the context of Nf1 haploinsufficiency.
claims.source: These findings suggest that LNAc dopamine and behavioral responses to unconditioned rewards are preserved in the context of Nf1 haploinsufficiency.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on reward consumption and social interaction experiments.

claims.claim: No differences in the number of licks during the CS, the number of anticipatory licks, or the learning rate were observed between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice during Pavlovian conditioning.
claims.source: No differences in the number of licks during the CS, the number of anticipatory licks, or the learning rate (the slope of the linear fit of CS licks across trials) were observed between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: dLight1.2 responses to the CS and US were enhanced and diminished, respectively, in mice that successfully learned the cue-reward association.
claims.source: Similar to previous studies (Patriarchi et al., 2018), dLight1.2 responses to the CS and US (Figure 4G) were enhanced and diminished, respectively, in mice that successfully learned the cue-reward association (i.e. the learning rate was correlated with the rate of change of each feature peak across trials; (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section with a citation to Patriarchi et al., 2018 and supported by data shown in Figure 4G-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Unexpected omission of the US following CS presentation after learning equivalently diminished the dopamine response to reward seeking in both Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ mice.
claims.source: Unexpected omission of the US following CS presentation after learning equivalently diminished the dopamine response to reward seeking in both Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ mice (Figure 4I), which is consistent with the role of dopamine in reward prediction error detection (Schultz et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section with a citation to Schultz et al., 2015 and supported by data shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- mice displayed enhanced dLight1.2 responses to CS presentation on the first day of testing compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
claims.source: Nf1+/- mice displayed enhanced dLight1.2 responses to CS presentation on the first day of testing (Figure 4J, inset) compared to Nf1+/+ littermates that was largest during the first trial (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The magnitude of the CS response on the first day of testing did not predict task performance in later sessions.
claims.source: The magnitude of the CS response on the first day of testing did not predict task performance in later sessions (Session one vs Session 10; Nf1+/+: R2 = 0.02, p=0.69; Nf1+/-: R2 = 0.0006, p=0.94).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section based on correlation analysis.

claims.claim: The ability to form cue-reward associations is equivalent between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- genotypes.
claims.source: These findings indicate that, although CS responses are larger in Nf1+/- mice, the ability to form cue-reward associations is equivalent between genotypes and coincides with adaptive changes in dopaminergic neurotransmission with learning.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on Pavlovian conditioning experiments.

claims.claim: Both Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice exhibited trial-by-trial increases in freezing during the first seven trials of cued fear conditioning that subsequently plateaued.
claims.source: Over the course of fifteen CS-US pairings, both Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice exhibited trial-by-trial increases in freezing during the first seven trials that subsequently plateaued (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: In both genotypes, the expression of freezing in later trials was correlated with the acquisition rate and the latency to freeze.
claims.source: In both genotypes, the expression of freezing in later trials (average freezing time, trials 8–15) was correlated with the acquisition rate (slope of the linear fit, trials 1–7; Figure 5B) and the latency to freeze (trials 8–15; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The freezing acquisition rate and average freezing time was lower in Nf1+/- mice compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
claims.source: Compared to Nf1+/+ littermates, both the acquisition rate and average freezing time was lower in Nf1+/- mice, which could be accounted for by an increased latency to freeze (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- mice had an increased latency to freeze during cued fear conditioning.
claims.source: Compared to Nf1+/+ littermates, both the acquisition rate and average freezing time was lower in Nf1+/- mice, which could be accounted for by an increased latency to freeze (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Presentation of the CS resulted in several seconds of locomotor stimulation in Nf1+/- mice that delayed freezing.
claims.source: Qualitative review of behavioral video recordings revealed that presentation of the CS resulted in several seconds of locomotor stimulation in Nf1+/- mice that delayed freezing (Video 1), whereas Nf1+/+ mice froze with short latency at CS onset once learning had occurred (Video 2).
claims.evidence: This observation is stated in the Results section and supported by Video 1.

claims.claim: A dopamine transient was observed at the onset of CS presentation that was greatest in trial 1, attenuated across trials, and was larger in Nf1+/- mice.
claims.source: During LNAc dLight1.2 monitoring, a dopamine transient was observed at the onset of CS presentation that was greatest in trial 1, attenuated across trials, and was larger in Nf1+/- mice (Figure 5D–E).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claims.claim: In Nf1+/- but not Nf1+/+ mice, the magnitude of the CS peak during trial one was negatively correlated with acquisition rate and freezing duration and positively correlated with latency to freeze.
claims.source: In Nf1+/- but not Nf1+/+ mice, the magnitude of the CS peak during trial one was negatively correlated with acquisition rate and freezing duration and positively correlated with latency to freeze (Figure 5F–G, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5F-G and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- mice had significantly larger initial US peak responses compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
claims.source: During US exposure, Nf1+/- mice had significantly larger initial US peak responses and a smaller integrated post-US rebound compared to Nf1+/+ littermates (area under the curve; Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- mice had a smaller integrated post-US rebound compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
claims.source: During US exposure, Nf1+/- mice had significantly larger initial US peak responses and a smaller integrated post-US rebound compared to Nf1+/+ littermates (area under the curve; Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In Nf1+/+ mice, the magnitude of the US anti-peak during trial one was negatively correlated with freezing and positively correlated with latency to freeze.
claims.source: In Nf1+/+ mice, the magnitude of the US anti-peak during trial one was negatively correlated with freezing and positively correlated with latency to freeze (Figure 5I–J, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5I-J and Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: The magnitude of the integrated post-US rebound was negatively correlated with the latency to freeze in Nf1+/- mice.
claims.source: Additionally, the magnitude of the integrated post-US rebound was negatively correlated with the latency to freeze in Nf1+/- mice (Figure 5I–J, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5I-J and Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: Both genotypes exhibited robust dopamine transients at the onset of the overhead light stimulus that returned to baseline within 1–2 s and decremented across trials.
claims.source: Both genotypes exhibited robust dopamine transients at the onset of the overhead light stimulus that returned to baseline within 1–2 s (Figure 6A) and decremented across trials (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 60 dB, 3 kHz auditory tone evoked dopamine transients at stimulus onset that were comparatively smaller than light responses and non-trial-dependent.
claims.source: In both Nf1+/+ mice and Nf1+/- mice, 60 dB, 3 kHz auditory tone evoked dopamine transients at stimulus onset (Figure 6B) that were comparatively smaller than light responses (Figure 6C) and non-trial-dependent (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6B-C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- mice exhibited larger responses to light but not tone onset.
claims.source: Nf1+/- mice exhibited larger responses to light but not tone onset (Figure 6C), which was confirmed when traces were analyzed as ΔF/F rather than z-score (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The development of cued freezing in Nf1+/- mice was equivalent to Nf1+/+ littermates across the first ten trials when a tone-only CS was used.
claims.source: We found that the development of cued freezing in Nf1+/- mice was equivalent to Nf1+/+ littermates across the first ten trials (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Addition of the overhead light stimulus to the CS was sufficient to perturb the expression of freezing in Nf1+/- but not Nf1+/+ mice by increasing the latency to freeze.
claims.source: Addition of the overhead light stimulus to the CS was sufficient to perturb the expression of freezing in Nf1+/- but not Nf1+/+ mice by increasing the latency to freeze (Figure 6E, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6E and Video 3.

claims.claim: Deficits in cued fear conditioning in Nf1+/- mice are reversible, visual stimulus-dependent, and independent of learning.
claims.source: Thus, deficits in cued fear conditioning in Nf1+/- mice are reversible, visual stimulus-dependent, and independent of learning.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on tone-only fear conditioning experiments.

claims.claim: Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice had similar reaction times to a looming stimulus.
claims.source: In response to the onset of the looming stimulus, both genotypes exhibited similar sub-second reaction times (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- mice were more likely to escape to the shelter at looming stimulus onset compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
claims.source: Compared to Nf1+/+ littermates, Nf1+/- mice were more likely to escape to the shelter at stimulus onset and exhibited shorter latencies to the first freezing episode (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Nf1+/- mice exhibited shorter latencies to the first freezing episode during looming stimulus presentation compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
claims.source: Compared to Nf1+/+ littermates, Nf1+/- mice were more likely to escape to the shelter at stimulus onset and exhibited shorter latencies to the first freezing episode (Figure 6F).

results.result: Nf1+/- mice exhibit reduced spontaneous dopamine transient event rate in the lateral nucleus accumbens (LNAc) compared to Nf1+/+ littermates, as measured by dLight1.2 fiber photometry. This reduction occurs without changes in baseline fluorescence, peak amplitude, FWHM, monoamine content, or tyrosine hydroxylase expression in striatal terminals.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 provide converging evidence from in vivo photometry (C31-C32) and biochemical/histological validation (C33-C34) that the reduced event rate is not due to terminal density or synthetic capacity changes (C35). The use of dLight1.2 with appropriate controls (isosbestic reference) and complementary HPLC/immunohistochemistry strengthens this conclusion.

results.result: Putative dopaminergic neurons in Nf1+/- VTA slices show reduced spontaneous firing rates and increased rheobase current requirement compared to Nf1+/+ neurons, supporting an activity-dependent mechanism for reduced dopamine transients. Action potential characteristics remain unchanged between genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 demonstrate consistent electrophysiological phenotypes using whole-cell patch clamp. The identification of dopaminergic neurons relied on AAV-PHP.eB-Th-GFP labeling and action potential duration (>1ms), which is a validated approach (C39). The inference that differences are activity-dependent (C38) is reasonable given the firing rate and rheobase data.

results.result: Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons in the VTA exhibit smaller soma size (reduced cross-sectional area, major and minor axis lengths) with proportionally increased input resistance and decreased membrane capacitance. These morphological changes are VTA-specific, with no differences observed in the substantia nigra pars compacta or in total VTA neuron counts.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C46 provide comprehensive morphological characterization using electrophysiology (C40-C41) and manual tracing of >2000 TH+ neurons per genotype (C42-C43). The VTA-specificity is demonstrated by negative findings in SNc (C45). The correlation between soma size and passive membrane properties is well-established in neuroscience, supporting the inference in C46.

results.result: Dendritic complexity and total neurite length are equivalent between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons, as assessed by Sholl analysis following Th-VAST labeling and neurite tracing.
results.evaluation: Claim C47 is supported by quantitative Sholl analysis shown in Figure 2H. The use of the novel Th-VAST system for sparse labeling enabled detailed morphological reconstruction. However, the specificity of Th-VAST was lower than expected (58.7% in VTA), which could introduce some uncertainty, though post-hoc TH confirmation was performed.

results.result: Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons show reduced Ih current amplitude that correlates with cell capacitance and is normalized when accounting for cell size. Forskolin treatment does not affect Ih magnitude or voltage dependence, suggesting the reduction is cAMP-independent and reflects smaller soma size rather than being causally related to reduced excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 systematically address whether Ih contributes to the excitability phenotype. The correlation analysis (C51), capacitance normalization (C50), and forskolin experiments (C52) provide strong evidence that Ih differences are secondary to soma size. The inference that this is unlikely to cause reduced excitability (C53) is reasonable but could benefit from additional functional validation.

results.result: Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons exhibit increased spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic current (sIPSC) frequency without changes in sIPSC amplitude or excitatory currents, indicating excitation/inhibition imbalance. Picrotoxin (GABAA antagonist) rescues spontaneous firing rates ex vivo, and morphine (μ-opioid receptor agonist) normalizes dLight1.2 transient rates in vivo, demonstrating that increased GABAergic tone gates dopaminergic excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57, C60-C61 provide strong mechanistic evidence through ex vivo pharmacology (picrotoxin rescue) and in vivo validation (morphine rescue). The use of both approaches strengthens the conclusion about excitation/inhibition imbalance. However, morphine acts systemically and could have effects beyond VTA GABA neurons, introducing some uncertainty about circuit specificity.

results.result: Morphine sulfate (5 mg/kg, s.c.) increases spontaneous dLight1.2 transient event rate in Nf1+/- mice without affecting event magnitude or FWHM.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 demonstrate pharmacological rescue of the baseline phenotype. The selective effect on event rate (not amplitude/FWHM) is consistent with the proposed mechanism of disinhibition. However, the comparison to Nf1+/+ baseline rates (mentioned in text but not shown in figure) would strengthen the claim of normalization.

results.result: Dopaminergic responses to unconditioned rewards (sucrose consumption and social interaction) are preserved in Nf1+/- mice, with no genotype differences in dLight1.2 transients, reward consumption, or social preference behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 demonstrate intact reward processing using multiple modalities (sucrose, social interaction). The convergence of photometry and behavioral measures supports the interpretation (C66) that unconditioned reward responses are preserved. This provides important context that the dopaminergic deficits are selective rather than global.

results.result: Nf1+/- mice show normal acquisition of cue-reward associations during Pavlovian conditioning, with equivalent licking behavior, learning rates, and adaptive changes in dopamine responses to CS and US across sessions. However, Nf1+/- mice exhibit enhanced dLight1.2 responses to CS presentation on the first day of testing, which does not predict later task performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 demonstrate preserved learning capacity despite altered initial CS responses. The correlation analyses (C68) and reward omission test (C69) validate that dopamine signals encode reward prediction errors appropriately in both genotypes. The enhanced initial CS response (C70) that doesn't predict performance (C71) suggests a salience rather than learning deficit.

results.result: During cued fear conditioning, Nf1+/- mice show reduced freezing acquisition and increased latency to freeze, associated with locomotor stimulation at CS onset. Nf1+/- mice exhibit larger dopamine transients to CS presentation that negatively correlate with freezing and positively correlate with freezing latency. US responses show larger initial peaks and smaller post-US rebounds in Nf1+/- mice, with genotype-specific correlations between dopamine features and behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C83 provide detailed characterization of fear conditioning phenotypes with simultaneous dopamine monitoring. The correlation analyses (C79, C82-C83) linking dopamine dynamics to behavior are compelling. However, the interpretation that enhanced CS responses cause delayed freezing (rather than both being consequences of another factor) requires caution. Video analysis (C77) provides qualitative support for the locomotor stimulation claim.

results.result: Nf1+/- mice exhibit selectively enhanced dopamine responses to overhead light but not auditory tone stimuli. Fear conditioning deficits in Nf1+/- mice are reversible and visual stimulus-dependent: freezing is normal with tone-only CS but disrupted when light is added, demonstrating that the phenotype is independent of learning ability.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 elegantly dissect the sensory modality specificity of the phenotype. The tone-only rescue experiment (C87-C88) provides strong evidence that the deficit is stimulus-specific rather than learning-related. The z-score and ΔF/F analyses both confirm the light-specific enhancement (C86), strengthening the conclusion.

results.result: In response to looming stimuli, Nf1+/- mice show similar reaction times to Nf1+/+ littermates but are more likely to escape to shelter and exhibit shorter latencies to first freezing episode, indicating enhanced defensive responses to threatening visual stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C92 demonstrate that enhanced visual stimulus responses extend to innate defensive behaviors. The preserved reaction time (C90) indicates intact sensory processing, while altered escape location and freezing latency (C91-C92) suggest differences in behavioral response selection or threat assessment.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of the ventral superior colliculus (vSC) produces time-locked dopamine release in the LNAc qualitatively similar to overhead light exposure and evokes escape behavior, demonstrating that the SC can drive rapid dopaminergic responses similar to those observed with visual stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 provide circuit-level evidence linking visual processing regions to dopamine release. The optogenetic approach directly tests the SC-VTA-NAc pathway. However, the experiment was performed in C57Bl/6N mice (not the Nf1 model), limiting direct mechanistic conclusions about the Nf1+/- phenotype. The inference (C95) is reasonable but would be strengthened by testing in Nf1+/- mice.

results.result: Optogenetic inhibition of VTA non-dopaminergic neurons (predominantly GABAergic) during looming stimulus presentation normalizes escape behavior and freezing latency in Nf1+/- mice to Nf1+/+ levels, demonstrating that VTA GABAergic neurons mediate the expression of enhanced visual stimulus responses caused by Nf1 haploinsufficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C101 provide strong causal evidence using intersectional genetics (Th-Cre with Cre-Off NpHR) to target non-dopaminergic VTA neurons. The specificity is validated by post-hoc analysis showing only 14.7% TH+ cells expressed NpHR (C96). The rescue of behavioral phenotypes (C98-C99) without affecting Nf1+/+ mice supports the mechanistic interpretation (C100-C101).

results.result: The authors propose that increased tonic inhibition reduces basal activity of Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons, while smaller soma volume acts as a compensatory mechanism to increase excitability during disinhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 present a mechanistic model integrating multiple findings. While C102 is well-supported by the data, C103 is speculative. The compensatory mechanism hypothesis would require additional experiments (e.g., testing whether preventing soma size reduction eliminates the phenotype, or measuring burst firing during disinhibition). The model is plausible but not directly tested.

results.result: Background claims establishing NF1 as an autosomal dominant disorder affecting ~1 in 3500 individuals, caused by loss of one NF1 gene copy, with cognitive symptoms in up to 70% of patients including ADHD in one-third. Prior mouse models show spatial learning deficits that are Ras/ERK-dependent and rescued by lovastatin, with evidence for dopaminergic involvement in the OPG model, though dopaminergic neurotransmission has never been investigated in vivo in NF1 models.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C28 provide literature context with appropriate citations. These establish the rationale for the study. The claim that dopaminergic neurotransmission has never been investigated in vivo (C28) is a strong statement that could be challenged if any prior in vivo dopamine measurements exist in NF1 models, though the authors likely mean real-time monitoring rather than tissue content measurements.

results.result: The dLight1.2 sensor allows sub-micromolar detection of extracellular dopamine with sub-second resolution and negligible sensitivity to other monoamines, GABA, and glutamate.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 describe the technical capabilities of dLight1.2 based on published characterization (Patriarchi et al., 2018; Corre et al., 2018). These are well-established properties of the sensor and appropriate for the application.

results.result: Discussion claims contextualizing findings within broader NF1 literature, including excitation/inhibition imbalance in multiple brain regions, differences between Nf1+/- and OPG models, therapeutic potential of GABAergic and dopaminergic interventions, visual processing deficits in human NF1 patients, and the role of superior colliculus in mediating visual stimulus responses through VTA circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C119 appropriately cite relevant literature to contextualize the findings. The comparisons between mouse models (C108-C113) help explain why some findings differ from prior work. The discussion of SC circuitry (C116-C119) integrates recent literature to propose mechanisms, though some connections are speculative.
